books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, B. Debating the Future of Slavery in America

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

stimulus.text: "The more I read, the more I was led to abhor and detest my enslavers. I could regard them in no other light than a band of successful robbers, who had left their homes, and gone to Africa, and stolen us from our homes, and in a strange land reduced us to slavery." — Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (Boston: Anti-Slavery Office, 1845), Chapter VII. Wording checked against the Project Gutenberg text and the UNC Documenting the American South edition.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Douglass, Narrative (1845)
stem: The passage best illustrates which of the following?

options.text: Enslaved people resisted by seeking knowledge their enslavers denied them
Enslavers encouraged enslaved people to read and write freely
options.misconception: Douglass's enslaver warned that learning would spoil a slave; reading was forbidden, not encouraged.

options.text: Douglass learned to read in a Massachusetts public school
options.misconception: Douglass learned in secret, trading bread for lessons; no public school taught him.

options.text: Reading was common among enslaved people across the South
options.misconception: Teaching enslaved people to read was banned in many Southern states; Douglass's learning was exceptional.

rationales.A: Douglass learned to read in secret, against his enslaver's orders, and used reading to argue against slavery. Knowledge itself was his resistance.
rationales.B: Master Hugh warned that learning would forever unfit a slave for slavery. Enslavers feared literacy, they did not encourage it.
rationales.C: No school taught Douglass. He learned from white playmates and from books he read in secret, trading food for lessons.
rationales.D: Southern states banned teaching enslaved people to read. Douglass's literacy was rare and dangerous, not common.
rationales.general:
1. Ask how Douglass learned. He learned in secret, against his enslaver's direct warning.
2. Ask what reading did. It gave him arguments against slavery and a hatred of it.
3. Name the pattern. Seeking forbidden knowledge was itself a form of resistance.
Background: In many Southern states it was illegal to teach an enslaved person to read or write.
Remember: when something is forbidden to a group, learning it anyway is resistance — ask who forbade it and why.
